Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
try hard not think about the trauma
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Michael, a 36-year-old European-American man married with no children, works in retail and has been struggling with post-traumatic stress symptoms since a man-made disaster that occurred six months ago. The event was a gas explosion at his local supermarket where he often shopped for groceries. Michael’s vivid memories of the disaster have been haunting him ever since, significantly impacting his daily life. The day of the explosion remains seared in Michael’s mind as fragmented snapshots. He recalls the cacophony of shattering glass and the acrid smell that permeated the air immediately after the blast. His memory of the event is so vivid that it feels more real than any other recollection, with each moment etched as a clear picture in his mind. When these memories surface, they trigger intense feelings of shame, making him feel like he bears responsibility for what happened. Michael’s work at the retail store has become increasingly challenging due to this trauma. The sight and texture of the plastic wrapping on the merchandise often remind him of the debris from the explosion. This tactile trigger brings back those haunting memories instantly. In response to these triggers, Michael employs maladaptive strategies that offer a brief reprieve but exacerbate his condition over time. When he feels overwhelmed by the memories and the accompanying shame, Michael resorts to magical thinking, telling himself repeatedly that the event did not really happen or was less severe than it actually was. He also tries to suppress thoughts about the trauma, burying them deep within his mind. However, when these suppression efforts fail, and the memories resurface, he turns to self-harm as a way to distract himself from the overwhelming emotions. The intensity of Michael’s shame on recall has only grown over time. Whenever he remembers the event, he feels an acute sense of guilt and embarrassment, which leads him to engage in more frequent episodes of magical thinking and suppressing thoughts about the trauma. This cycle becomes self-reinforcing; as his memories become more vivid and real, his maladaptive coping mechanisms intensify. Michael’s wife has noticed changes in his behavior but struggles to understand why he pulls away from her when they pass by the supermarket or even discuss it. She sees him physically wince whenever he encounters textures reminiscent of that fateful day. These triggers have led him to avoid certain areas and situations, including parts of his job where such textures are unavoidable. The traumatic event’s lasting impact is not just psychological; Michael's work performance has slipped due to frequent absences and a noticeable drop in concentration. His self-harm behaviors, though occasional, have left visible marks on his body, causing further distress as he worries about being caught by his colleagues or family. Despite the overwhelming nature of these symptoms, what finally prompted Michael to seek help was an incident at work where a customer’s aggressive behavior reminded him of the misbehavior that contributed to the disaster. He felt unable to cope with this trigger and feared it might lead to another episode of self-harm. Michael is most afraid of losing control and hurting himself or others, but he hopes therapy will help him regain a sense of normalcy in his daily life. The combination of triggers, maladaptive strategies, and intense memories has created a cycle that feels inescapable for Michael. He is determined to break this cycle and find healthier ways to manage the trauma’s aftermath.
